15550: A surplice is a loose, white garment worn by certain people during Christian religious services. Think of it as a special piece of clothing that signals, "I have a role in this ceremony."

Picture a wide, flowing white top — almost like an oversized white shirt or a short white robe. It falls roughly to the hips or knees, depending on the tradition. Its most distinctive feature is its wide, flowing sleeves, which are noticeably roomier than a normal shirt's sleeves. The fabric is typically white linen or cotton, and in some traditions, the hem and sleeves are decorated with lace or embroidery. Overall, it gives an impression of flowing, ceremonial whiteness.

A surplice is worn during church services, mainly in Western Christian traditions such as Roman Catholic, Anglican/Episcopal, and Lutheran churches. The people most commonly seen wearing one include:

  • Clergy — priests, deacons, and ministers
  • Choir members — the singers who perform during the service
  • Altar servers (acolytes) — people who assist the priest at the altar
  • Lay readers — non-clergy members who read scripture aloud during the service

It is not everyday clothing. It is put on specifically for the duration of a religious ceremony and taken off afterward.

A surplice is almost never worn alone as the only garment. It is layered on top of other vestments (the general word for special religious clothing). Most commonly, it goes over a cassock — a long, plain robe that extends all the way to the floor, usually black or dark-coloured. The white surplice over the dark cassock is one of the most recognizable sights in a traditional church choir or clergy procession.

The white colour is symbolic. In Christian tradition, white stands for purity, holiness, and consecration (being set apart for a sacred purpose). By wearing a surplice, the person is visually marking themselves as someone who is set apart from the congregation for a specific role in the service. It is a uniform, in a sense — one that communicates both function and reverence.
How it differs from similar garments

Since a surplice is one of several white religious garments, it helps to know what it is not:

  • An alb is also a white garment, but it is a full-length robe reaching all the way to the feet, more form-fitting, and typically worn by the priest specifically for the Eucharist (Communion). A surplice is shorter and much looser.
  • A chasuble is a large, poncho-like outer vestment worn over everything else by a priest celebrating Mass. It is usually colourful (not white by default) and shaped very differently.
  • A cope is a long, cape-like ceremonial cloak. Very different in shape.

The surplice is specifically the shorter, wide-sleeved, loose white layer worn by choir members, acolytes, and lesser clergy — not typically the main celebrant's most formal vestment.

The choirboys straightened their surplices before filing into the cathedral.

The deacon wore a black cassock beneath his white surplice.

She had worn a surplice as an altar server throughout her childhood.

A surplice is a loose, wide-sleeved, white liturgical garment worn over a cassock by clergy, choir members, and altar servers during Christian worship services, symbolizing purity and a designated role in the ceremony.
15551: When "surplus" is used as an adjective, it describes something that exists in a quantity greater than what is needed, used, or required. It is the word that describes the "leftover" or "excess" portion — the amount that remains after every need has already been fully satisfied.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine you are cooking rice for 4 people, but you accidentally cook enough for 7. After all 4 people eat until they are full, there is rice left in the pot. That remaining rice is the surplus rice — it was produced beyond what the situation actually needed.

This is the heart of the word. "Surplus" always points to the gap between what was needed and what actually exists — and that gap is always in the direction of having more than enough.

Using "surplus" as an adjective isn't just about saying something is "extra." It carries a specific, precise idea: the quantity exceeded a measurable requirement. There is always a reference point — a need, a demand, a use — and surplus describes everything that lies beyond that point.

This is why the word is very common in formal, economic, and official settings. A household might say they have "extra food," but a government food agency would say it has surplus food supplies, because the excess is being measured against a specific, calculated need.

Surplus food refers to food that has been grown, produced, or stored in amounts beyond what people can consume or what the market demands. Governments often store surplus grain to prepare for famines.

Surplus money or funds means money that remains after all costs, expenses, and obligations have been paid. A company that earns more than it spends is said to have a surplus budget.

Surplus stock or inventory refers to goods a business has produced or purchased in quantities that exceed customer demand. Shops sometimes sell surplus stock at a discount to clear space.

Surplus labor describes a situation where there are more available workers than there are jobs or tasks that need to be done.

Surplus equipment means tools, machinery, or supplies that are no longer needed because the purpose they served has been completed or eliminated. The military, for example, regularly auctions off surplus vehicles and gear.

The adjective itself is neutral — it simply states a fact about quantity. But depending on the context, the implications can lean either way.

It can be a good thing: a country having surplus food reserves is well-prepared for a crisis. A company with a surplus budget is financially healthy. A city with surplus water storage is protected against drought.

It can be a problem: surplus labor in an economy can mean high unemployment. Surplus inventory for a business may mean they spent money producing things nobody wanted. Surplus waste means more material than can be safely processed or disposed of.

So the word itself is not good or bad — the situation it describes determines that.

This is where the word gets sharper and more precise. Several English words are close in meaning, but they are not identical.

Extra is the most casual, everyday version of this idea. You might say "an extra chair" without thinking much about it. "Surplus" is more deliberate and formal — it implies that the excess has been recognized relative to a specific, defined need.

Excess is the closest word to "surplus," and they are often interchangeable. However, "excess" tends to carry a slightly stronger negative tone, suggesting something has gone too far or is undesirable — as in "excess spending" or "excess weight." "Surplus" is more neutral and does not judge the excess as necessarily bad.

Spare implies something deliberately kept in reserve for a possible future need. A spare tire is intentionally saved for when you might need it. Surplus, by contrast, does not require intention — it simply describes what is left over, whether planned or not.

Leftover is informal and usually used for small, everyday things like food after a meal. Surplus operates in broader, more formal contexts and implies a calculated or notable excess.

Remaining simply means "what is still left," without the specific idea of exceeding a need. If you have 3 apples remaining, that doesn't tell you whether it's more or less than you needed. "Surplus" specifically tells you the remaining amount exceeds the requirement.

Whenever you see or want to use "surplus" as an adjective, ask yourself: Is this thing in excess of what was needed or used? If the answer is yes, "surplus" fits perfectly. The word is always describing the portion that goes beyond the threshold of need — the overflow, the overhang, the amount that the requirement simply couldn't absorb.
15552:
A surplus is the amount of something that is left over after all the need for it has been met.

Think of it this way: you have a certain amount of something — money, food, goods, energy. There is also a certain amount that is needed or used. If what you have is greater than what you need or use, the leftover portion is the surplus.

Surplus = The Total You Have − The Total You Need/Use

The key idea is that a surplus only exists in relation to a need, a demand, or a requirement. It is not just "a lot of something." It is specifically more than enough of something — the portion beyond the point of sufficiency.

Imagine you bake 20 cookies for a party, expecting 20 guests. But only 15 guests show up, and each person eats exactly one cookie.

  • Cookies baked: 20
  • Cookies needed: 15
  • Cookies left over: 5

Those 5 extra cookies are your surplus. You had more than what the situation required.

Now here's something important to notice: the surplus didn't exist because you had a lot of cookies. It existed because you had more than enough cookies relative to the demand. If 25 guests had shown up, you would have had a shortage — the exact opposite of a surplus.

The word "surplus" is used in many areas of life. Here are the most common ones:

1. Money and Budgets
When a government, a business, or a household earns or receives more money than it spends, the extra money is a surplus. For example, if a city collects $10 million in taxes but only spends $8 million on services, it has a budget surplus of $2 million. This leftover money can be saved or used elsewhere.

2. Trade Between Countries
When a country sells more goods to other countries than it buys from them, the difference in value is called a trade surplus. For example, if Japan exports $500 billion worth of goods but only imports $400 billion worth, it has a trade surplus of $100 billion.

3. Food and Agriculture
When farmers grow more food than the population consumes, the leftover stock is a food surplus. Governments sometimes store surplus grain in reserves, or donate it to other regions.

4. Production and Supply
When factories or industries produce more of a product than the market wants to buy, the unsold stock is a surplus. For instance, if car manufacturers produce 1 million cars but consumers only buy 800,000, the remaining 200,000 cars are a surplus in the market.

5. Energy
When a power grid generates more electricity than is being consumed at any given moment, the extra electricity is an energy surplus. This is a growing topic in discussions about solar and wind energy.

It's worth pausing on something subtle but important. The English word "extra" is casual and loose — it just means additional. But "surplus" carries a more precise meaning. It implies:

  • There was a specific need, demand, or requirement being measured against.
  • That need has been fully met.
  • What remains after fully meeting that need is the surplus.

So a surplus is not just an abundance or a large quantity. A warehouse stacked high with goods is not automatically a surplus — if all of those goods are needed and will be used, there is no surplus. The surplus only appears when supply outstrips demand.
Surplus as a Positive or a Problem

A surplus is not always a good thing or a bad thing — it depends on the context.

When a surplus is good: A budget surplus means a government is financially responsible and has money to save or invest. A food surplus means no one goes hungry, and there's a reserve for difficult times.

When a surplus is a problem: A surplus of goods in a market can cause prices to fall because sellers have to compete to get rid of the excess. A surplus of labour (more workers than available jobs) leads to unemployment. Too much of something — even something good — can create its own complications.

The direct opposite of a surplus is a deficit (sometimes also called a shortfall or shortage). A deficit occurs when what you have is less than what you need. If that same city collected $8 million in taxes but needed to spend $10 million, it would have a budget deficit of $2 million. Understanding surplus becomes even clearer when you hold it against its opposite.
A surplus is the amount by which what you have or produce exceeds what is needed or used — it is the leftover that remains after every requirement has been fully satisfied.
15553:
To surprise someone means to do something, say something, or appear somewhere at a moment they were not expecting — causing them to feel a sudden jolt of astonishment, shock, or wonder. The one essential ingredient is unexpectedness. Without that, there is no surprise.

Think of it this way: surprise lives in the gap between what someone expected and what actually happened. The bigger that gap, the stronger the surprise.

1. To cause someone to feel astonishment or wonder

This is the most common use. You give someone information, do something for them, or reveal something they were not prepared for — and this makes them react with shock, disbelief, or delight.

  • "Her decision to resign surprised everyone." (No one expected it.)
  • "The ending of the movie surprised me." (I didn't see it coming.)
  • "He surprised his mother by cleaning the entire house." (She never expected him to do it.)

Importantly, the word surprise is emotionally neutral on its own. The surprise can be pleasant or unpleasant — context tells you which.

  • Pleasant: "She surprised him with a beautiful birthday cake."
  • Unpleasant: "The sudden news of layoffs surprised the workers."
  • Pure shock: "The earthquake's power surprised even the scientists."

2. To come upon someone suddenly and unexpectedly

Here, to surprise someone means to find, discover, or catch them in a situation before they realize you are there. You arrive without warning.

  • "The officer surprised the thief as he was breaking into the car." (The thief had no idea the officer was coming.)
  • "I surprised my cat sitting on top of the refrigerator." (I walked in and found her there unexpectedly.)
  • "The manager surprised her staff by arriving two hours early." (They didn't know she was coming.)

This sense is often — though not always — used when someone is caught doing something they shouldn't be doing.

Surprise is a transitive verb, which means it always needs a direct object — a person or thing being surprised. You cannot just say "I surprised." You must say who or what was surprised.

Here are the main patterns:

→ surprise + someone
"The news surprised her."
"Your question surprised me."

→ surprise + someone + with + something
Used when doing something unexpected, often something nice, for someone.
"He surprised her with flowers."
"They surprised the teacher with a farewell party."

→ surprise + someone + by + doing something
"She surprised me by arriving three hours early."
"He surprised his boss by finishing the project ahead of schedule."

→ surprise + someone + doing something
Used when you catch someone in the middle of an action.
"I surprised him reading my private letters." (I walked in and found him doing it.)
"She surprised the children sneaking cookies from the jar."

→ It + surprises + someone + that…
"It surprised me that no one had noticed the mistake."
"It doesn't surprise him that she left."

This is extremely important — it is very commonly used in everyday English. When you are on the receiving end of surprise, when you feel it, the passive form is used.

  • "I was surprised by his reaction." (His reaction caused the feeling in me.)
  • "She was surprised to find the door unlocked."
  • "We were surprised when they cancelled the event."
  • "Don't be surprised if it doesn't work." (A warning: prepare yourself for the possibility of failure.)

The passive pairs with two prepositions:

Surprised by — the most common. Focuses on what caused the feeling.
"I was surprised by her silence."

Surprised at — also correct. Often carries a slight tone of disapproval or judgment, especially when directed at a person's behavior.
"I'm surprised at your behavior."
"He was surprised at how quickly time had passed."

Both are grammatically correct. Use either freely, but keep in mind that "surprised at someone" can sound like mild criticism.

You can modify how strongly the surprise is felt:

  • Mild: "I was mildly surprised," "a little surprised," "somewhat surprised."
  • Moderate: "quite surprised," "rather surprised."
  • Strong: "deeply surprised," "genuinely surprised," "completely taken aback."

One especially useful phrase: "pleasantly surprised."
This means you expected something bad, mediocre, or nothing at all — but what you got was actually good.
"I was pleasantly surprised by how delicious the cheap restaurant was."

You can also surprise yourself — this means you did something you didn't think you were capable of, or you felt something you didn't expect to feel.

  • "I surprised myself by staying calm during the argument." (I didn't expect to be that calm.)
  • "She surprised herself by enjoying a sport she always thought she'd hate."
A Tricky But Important Construction: "Wouldn't Be Surprised If…"

This is subtle and worth learning carefully. When someone says:

"I wouldn't be surprised if he quits next week."

It actually means: I think it is quite likely that he will quit. It sounds cautious and modest, but it is actually used to express a fairly confident expectation. It is a polite, indirect way of saying "I think this will probably happen."

  • "I wouldn't be surprised if they cancel the event." (= I think they probably will.)
  • "It wouldn't surprise me if she wins." (= I think she quite likely will win.)

The logic: if you wouldn't be surprised, it means the outcome would not feel unexpected to you — which means you're already half-expecting it.

To surprise someone = to do something, reveal something, or appear somewhere they were not prepared for, causing a sudden feeling of astonishment — or to discover and catch them in a moment before they know you are there.
15554:
Surreal describes something that is real — it's actually happening — but feels like a dream. Your mind knows it's real, yet something about it refuses to feel real. Reality seems to have bent its own rules for a moment.

That gap — between what is happening and what your mind can accept as happening — is exactly what surreal captures.

When something is surreal, there's usually a sense of disorientation, as if you're watching yourself from outside your own body, or as if the world has briefly paused its normal logic. Time can feel strange. Your emotions might not arrive immediately. You might catch yourself thinking: This can't actually be happening.

It can feel magical. It can feel unsettling. It can feel like both at once.

Surreal tends to come up at the edges of normal experience — moments so extreme, unexpected, or impossible-seeming that the ordinary feeling of "yes, this is real life" slips away:

  • Hearing shocking news about someone you love
  • Winning something huge after years of trying
  • Standing somewhere you've only ever seen in photographs
  • Being caught in an event so dramatic it looks like a film set
  • A city street completely flooded, with cars floating past — you're there, it's real, but nothing about it feels like it should exist

In each case, reality hasn't stopped. But the feeling of reality has.
A key detail: surreal doesn't mean fake

This is important. Surreal doesn't mean something didn't happen or isn't true. It means that even though it happened, it carries a dreamlike quality. The person who says "it felt surreal" isn't doubting what they witnessed — they're describing the strange texture of experiencing it.

You can use it in three connected ways:

  1. A feeling or experience — "The whole ceremony felt surreal. I kept waiting to wake up."
  2. A scene or place — "The abandoned hospital had a surreal, unsettling atmosphere." (The place itself looks like it's out of a dream.)
  3. A situation or sequence of events — "In a surreal turn of events, the man I'd been looking for showed up at my door." (The situation is so strange and coincidental it defies normal logic.)
How strong a word is it?

Surreal is a strong word. You wouldn't use it for something mildly surprising. It belongs to moments when reality feels genuinely warped — when your mind needs time to catch up with what's in front of it. If something is just a little unusual, "strange" or "odd" is plenty. Reach for surreal when the strangeness has a dreamlike, unmooring quality to it.
How it differs from similar words

Strange / weird / odd — These just mean unusual. Surreal goes much deeper. It's not that something is merely unusual — it's that reality itself seems to have distorted.

Bizarre — Something bizarre is very strange, often in an almost absurd or ridiculous way. But bizarre doesn't carry the dreamlike quality. A clown juggling on a subway is bizarre. Waking up to find your city underwater is surreal.

Dreamlike — This is the closest word to surreal, and they overlap heavily. The difference is in feel: dreamlike tends to be soft, hazy, and gentle — floating through a fog. Surreal has a sharper edge. It can be unsettling, disorienting, or deeply strange. All surreal things have a dreamlike quality, but not everything dreamlike is quite surreal.

Unreal — "Unreal" can simply mean impressive or hard to believe: "That performance was unreal!" Surreal is more specific — it means reality feels distorted in a dreamlike way. It's about how the world feels, not just how impressive something is.

Absurd — Absurd means illogical or pointless in a way that exposes life's randomness. Surreal and absurd can overlap (a situation can be both), but surreal focuses on the perceptual strangeness — how it feels to be inside that moment — while absurd focuses on the logic (or lack of it).

Surreal is emotionally neutral. The word itself carries no judgment. It can describe:

  • Something beautiful and overwhelming: "Seeing the Northern Lights in person for the first time was surreal."
  • Something deeply unsettling: "Walking through the city after the earthquake was surreal — silence where there had been noise."
  • Something joyful but hard to believe: "Holding my child for the first time felt surreal."

The word only tells you about the dreamlike, reality-bending quality of an experience — not whether that experience was good or bad.

"The whole thing felt surreal — I kept expecting to wake up."

"The abandoned town had a surreal, ghostly atmosphere."

"Surreal doesn't even begin to describe it: the person I'd been searching for walked in right as I gave up."

"It was a surreal moment — the two rivals, both crying, standing side by side."
The one-sentence definition to hold onto

Surreal describes something real that feels like a dream — where reality is happening, but your mind struggles to fully accept it as real, because it's too strange, too intense, too unexpected, or too impossible-seeming to fit neatly into the ordinary feeling of everyday life.
15555:
Surrealism is a style in art, literature, film, and other creative fields where the normal rules of reality are deliberately abandoned. Things that could never exist or happen in the real world are shown as if they're completely ordinary. A clock melts like warm wax. A man's face is replaced by a floating apple. A train bursts out of a fireplace. Time, space, and logic dissolve.

The result feels like being inside a dream — vivid and detailed, yet deeply strange and impossible to fully explain.

Surrealism began as a formal movement in France in the 1920s. A French writer named André Breton launched it officially in 1924 through a document called the Surrealist Manifesto, which explained what surrealism was and what it was trying to achieve.

The movement was heavily influenced by Sigmund Freud, the famous Austrian thinker who had argued that the human mind has a hidden layer — the unconscious — where suppressed desires, fears, memories, and fantasies live. Most of the time, the rational, logical side of our brain keeps that hidden layer locked away. Dreams are the main window into it.

Surrealists believed that this unconscious part of the mind held a richer, deeper, and more truthful version of human experience than the controlled, rational mind ever could. Their goal was to break free from the grip of reason and logic, and let the unconscious speak freely. They believed that only by escaping rational thought could humans reach what they called a higher or surreality — a reality that was more complete because it included the dream world alongside the waking world.
What Surrealism Looks Like in Art

The most famous surrealist artists are Salvador Dalí and René Magritte, and their paintings are perhaps the clearest windows into what surrealism is.

Salvador Dalí painted images that feel like windows directly into a dream. His most famous work, The Persistence of Memory (1931), shows soft, drooping clocks draped over hard surfaces in a barren, sun-bleached landscape. Nothing in the painting follows the laws of physics, yet every detail is painted in a precise, hyper-realistic style. That contrast — photographic realism applied to a completely impossible scene — creates a deeply unsettling effect. You can almost feel the wrongness of it, the way a nightmare feels wrong even as you're in it.

René Magritte was a Belgian painter who loved placing ordinary objects in bizarre, impossible contexts. His painting The Son of Man shows a neatly dressed businessman wearing a bowler hat — but a large green apple floats in front of his face, hiding it. His famous The Treachery of Images shows a painted pipe with the words "Ceci n'est pas une pipe" (French for "This is not a pipe") written beneath it, pointing out that a picture of a thing is not the thing itself. Magritte's work constantly plays with perception, identity, and the gap between appearances and reality.

Other significant surrealist artists include Max Ernst, Joan Miró, Giorgio de Chirico, and Man Ray. Frida Kahlo is often grouped with surrealists too, though she personally resisted the label — her paintings draw heavily on her own pain, identity, and Mexican culture, but share surrealism's dreamlike, symbolic quality.
What Surrealism Looks Like in Writing

In literature, the goal is the same — bypass logic, let the unconscious out — but the methods are different from painting.

Surrealist writers often used a technique called automatic writing: the writer tries to turn off the conscious, deliberate, editing part of the brain and simply let words flow without controlling them. The theory was that this unfiltered stream of words would reveal the unconscious mind directly. The results are often fragmented, associative, and dreamlike — ideas connected not by logic but by feeling, rhythm, or hidden emotional links.

André Breton himself wrote novels and poetry in this style. His semi-autobiographical novel Nadja (1928) describes a strange, intense relationship with a mysterious woman, mixing real events with dreamlike episodes, blurring the boundary between documentation and imagination.
What Surrealism Looks Like in Film

Surrealism found a powerful home in cinema as well. The director Luis Buñuel, working with Salvador Dalí, made one of the most famous examples of surrealist film: Un Chien Andalou ("An Andalusian Dog," 1929). It has no coherent plot — just a sequence of disturbing, dreamlike images strung together to unsettle the viewer and destroy their rational expectations. There is no "meaning" to decode in a logical sense. The film works like a dream works: through association, shock, and feeling.

Later filmmakers deeply influenced by surrealism include David Lynch (Eraserhead, Mulholland Drive), Jean Cocteau, and Michel Gondry.

Across all these fields, surrealism relies on a consistent set of methods:

Juxtaposition — placing two completely unrelated things side by side to create a jarring, strange, or thought-provoking effect. A burning giraffe standing calmly on a city street. A telephone whose handset is replaced by a lobster (this is an actual Dalí sculpture).

Dreamlike logic — events and images connect through emotion or hidden association rather than cause and effect. Things happen because they feel linked, not because one logically causes the other.

The uncanny — taking something completely familiar and making it feel deeply, wrongly strange. A room you know but that suddenly feels like it shouldn't exist. A face you recognise but that now seems threatening. This eerie quality — the familiar made alien — is central to surrealism.

Automatism — creating without deliberate control. The hand draws or writes freely, the conscious mind steps back, and what emerges is taken as a direct expression of the unconscious.

Transformation — objects, people, and environments melt into, morph into, or merge with one another without explanation or logical cause.

The Exquisite Corpse — a playful surrealist game (and creative technique) where several people collaborate on a drawing or piece of writing without seeing what the others have done. One person draws a head and folds the paper; the next draws a body without seeing the head; the next draws legs. The result is an impossible, disjointed creature. The game illustrates the surrealist belief that bypassing conscious coordination reveals something truer and more interesting than deliberate, controlled collaboration.

Two common confusions are worth clearing up.

Surrealism is not just "weird for the sake of being weird." It has a serious philosophical purpose: to access a deeper layer of human experience by freeing the mind from rational control. The strangeness is deliberate and meaningful, not random.

Surrealism is not fantasy. Fantasy creates entirely imaginary worlds with their own internal logic and rules — dragons, magic kingdoms, invented physics. Surrealism takes this world, the real one you recognize, and distorts it in ways that feel emotionally true even when they're logically impossible. The landscapes in Dalí's paintings are recognizable — a beach, a desert, a table — but something is terribly, impossibly wrong with them.

Many surrealists, including Breton, held strong left-wing political beliefs. They saw the liberation of the unconscious mind as connected to a broader liberation of human beings from oppressive social and political systems. If rigid, authoritarian structures in society suppressed human freedom, then the rigid, authoritarian structures of rational thought in art suppressed creative freedom in the same way. Surrealism was not just an aesthetic movement — it was, for many of its founders, a revolutionary act.

This political dimension faded as the movement broke apart (most significantly after World War II), but it explains why surrealists were often confrontational and provocative, not just eccentric.
How the Word Is Used Today

"Surrealism" is used in two ways today.

In its strict, historical sense, it refers specifically to the 20th-century movement described above. Art critics, historians, and academics use it this way: "Magritte's work is a central achievement of surrealism."

In its loose, everyday sense, "surrealism" (and especially its adjective form, surreal) is used to describe anything that feels strangely dreamlike, disorienting, or impossible — even if it has nothing to do with the original movement. When people say "the whole experience was surreal" or "that film has a surrealist quality," they usually mean the thing felt unreal, bizarre, or eerily out of step with normal waking life — the way a vivid dream feels when you're in it.

This everyday use has become so common that it now almost functions as a separate meaning: surrealism = a quality of dreamlike, disorienting strangeness.
A Summary to Tie It All Together

Surrealism is both a creative movement and a quality. As a movement (born in 1920s France), it was a deliberate attempt to bypass rational thought, tap into the unconscious mind, and use dreams, impossible images, and free association to reveal a deeper human truth. As a quality, it describes anything that blurs the line between reality and dream — vivid, strange, illogical, and yet somehow deeply felt.

It is the art of making the impossible feel inevitable, and the familiar feel alien. It says: reason does not own the whole of human experience. The dream world is real too.
15556: To surrender means to stop resisting and give in — either to a person, a force, a situation, or even a feeling. Think of it as the moment when you decide (or are forced) to stop fighting and accept that the other side, or something beyond your control, has the upper hand.

1. To stop fighting and yield to an opponent or authority

This is the most classic use. When soldiers lay down their weapons and raise a white flag, they surrender. They are saying: "We give up. You have won. We will no longer resist you." The same idea applies outside of war. A criminal who walks into a police station and turns himself in has surrendered to the authorities. A debater who runs out of arguments and admits the other person is right has surrendered the argument.

The key element here is resistance followed by the giving up of that resistance. You cannot truly surrender if you were never resisting in the first place.

The enemy army surrendered after three days of battle.
He finally surrendered to the police after hiding for a week.
She refused to surrender, even when she knew she had already lost.

2. To give up or hand over something you possess

You can surrender an object, a right, a position, or a claim — meaning you give it up, usually because an authority demands it or circumstances force you to. The thing you surrender is something you had control over, and you are now giving that control away.

Passengers were asked to surrender their passports at the border.
The company surrendered its license after failing to meet safety standards.
He surrendered his seat on the board when the scandal broke out.
They surrendered the territory they had captured during the war.

Notice that in this sense, surrender is stronger than simply "giving" something. It always carries the sense that you are giving up something you held, valued, or had a right to — often reluctantly, under pressure, or as a consequence of defeat.

3. To give yourself over completely to a feeling, experience, or force

This is the figurative, more emotional use of the word. When you stop fighting a feeling and let it wash over you completely, you surrender to it. This use is very common in literature, poetry, and everyday emotional language.

Exhausted after the long journey, she finally surrendered to sleep.
He tried to stay composed, but eventually surrendered to laughter.
Don't surrender to despair — things will get better.
She surrendered herself completely to the music and forgot the world.

In this sense, surrender is not always negative. Surrendering to joy, to laughter, to rest — these can be beautiful things. The word simply means you have stopped holding back and have allowed something to take over.

One of the most important nuances of this word is that surrender can be either forced or chosen.

When it is forced, you surrender because you have no real choice — you are overpowered, outmatched, or cornered.

Outnumbered ten to one, the garrison had no choice but to surrender.

When it is chosen, you voluntarily give up — perhaps because you realize the fight is pointless, because it is the right thing to do, or because continuing would cause more harm.

Rather than prolong the legal battle, she chose to surrender her claim to the inheritance.
He surrendered voluntarily, hoping for a lighter sentence.

Both are "surrendering," but the emotional and moral weight is very different. A forced surrender feels like defeat. A chosen surrender can feel like wisdom, relief, or even courage.
Grammar: How the Word Works in a Sentence

Surrender is flexible in how it appears in a sentence.

Used without an object (you are the one giving up):

The troops surrendered at dawn.

Surrender + something (you give up a specific thing):

She surrendered her weapons.

Surrender + to + someone/something (you yield to a person, authority, or force):

He surrendered to the police. / She surrendered to grief.

Surrender + yourself + to (you give yourself over completely):

They surrendered themselves to the mercy of the court.

Surrender + something + to + someone (you hand something over to a specific person):

The thieves surrendered the stolen goods to the detective.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Surrender is not a neutral word. It almost always carries emotional weight because it implies that something was at stake — a fight, a possession, a right, a feeling. Depending on the context, surrender can feel like:

Defeat and humiliation — when an army lays down its arms, surrender can feel like the worst possible outcome.

Relief and release — when you have been fighting exhaustion, grief, or an impossible situation, surrender can feel like finally letting go of a burden that was too heavy to carry.

Wisdom or grace — in certain spiritual and philosophical traditions, the ability to surrender one's ego, pride, or desire for control is seen as a sign of maturity and inner strength, not weakness.

This is why the word appears so often in both contexts of war and of deep personal emotion — it captures the universal human experience of reaching the limits of one's resistance.
How Surrender Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close to surrender, but they are not identical.

Yield is very close to surrender, and the two are often interchangeable. However, yield tends to suggest a gentler, more gradual giving way — like water yielding to a rock — whereas surrender often implies a more decisive, complete act of giving up after resistance.

Give up is the most casual and informal equivalent. It is broader and less dramatic. You can "give up" on a hobby without any real fight involved. Surrender almost always implies that something meaningful was at stake and that there was a genuine struggle before the giving up.

Submit focuses more on accepting the authority or rules of someone else, not necessarily after a fight. You submit a form, submit to a law, submit to a medical procedure. Surrender has more of a sense of active resistance that ends.

Capitulate is a formal word that means almost exactly the same as surrender, but it is used almost exclusively in the context of negotiations, conflicts, or debates — and it always implies that the person resisted for a while before finally giving in.

Relinquish means to give up something you hold or have a right to, but without the sense of struggle or defeat. You relinquish a role, a title, or a claim — it is more administrative and less emotional than surrender.

Concede means to acknowledge that something is true or that the other side has a point or has won. It is narrower than surrender — you can concede a point in an argument without surrendering the entire argument.

Surrender is not the same as simply losing. You can lose a battle while still fighting with everything you have. Surrender is the active, conscious act of stopping the resistance. A soldier who is killed in battle has not surrendered. A soldier who lays down his weapon and walks toward the enemy with hands raised has.

Surrender is also not just "giving." When you give someone a gift, there is no sense of struggle, defeat, or yielding. Surrender always carries the idea that something was being held, defended, or resisted — and then let go.
To surrender means to stop resisting and give in — whether that means laying down weapons before an enemy, handing over something you held, or letting a powerful feeling take over you completely.
15557:
Surreptitious means doing something secretly and carefully, specifically because you know that if someone noticed, they would disapprove, stop you, or get you in trouble.

It's not just about being secret. It's about being sneaky in a guilty, cautious way — like you're fully aware that what you're doing is not allowed or not acceptable, so you're trying hard not to get caught.

Every time you see or use this word, there are two ideas working together:

Secrecy + the awareness that it's wrong or forbidden.

Remove either one, and the word no longer fits. A surprise party is secret, but it's not surreptitious — nobody feels guilty about it. A surreptitious act always carries that quiet sense of "I know I shouldn't be doing this."

These examples will make it click instantly:

  • A student takes a surreptitious glance at a classmate's test paper during an exam. He isn't openly cheating — he's carefully, guiltily stealing a quick look, hoping nobody sees him.
  • A child sneaks a surreptitious bite of the cake before the guests arrive. She does it fast, looking over her shoulder, knowing her mother would scold her.
  • The employee sent a surreptitious text message under the desk during the meeting. He kept his phone low, his eyes half on the screen, trying not to get caught.
  • She gave him a surreptitious smile across the room — just a tiny, quick one that the others weren't supposed to notice.

Notice what all these have in common: the person is trying very hard to avoid being seen, and the reason is always that guilt or awareness of wrongdoing (or at least rule-breaking).

This is important, because knowing where a word doesn't apply sharpens your understanding of where it does.

  • A spy on a classified mission is operating in secret — but we'd call it covert, not surreptitious. Covert is neutral and professional. Surreptitious has a more personal, guilty, almost ashamed quality to it.
  • A ninja moving silently through shadows is being stealthy — focused on physical silence and invisibility. Surreptitious is less about physical skill and more about the intention to hide something you know is questionable.
  • A child's birthday surprise is secret but perfectly innocent. No guilt, no wrongdoing — so it is not surreptitious.
Similar Words and How Surreptitious Differs

Furtive is the closest word to surreptitious, and they are often interchangeable. However, furtive more often describes a manner, glance, or look — the body language of someone who's scared of being caught. Surreptitious more often describes the act or action itself. A person gives a furtive glance; they perform a surreptitious act. In practice though, this line is thin, and both are perfectly acceptable in most contexts.

Sneaky is the casual, everyday version of surreptitious. If surreptitious is the formal, sophisticated word you'd find in a novel or a newspaper, sneaky is the version you'd use in everyday conversation. Same idea, different register.
The Tone and Register of This Word

Surreptitious is a formal word. You'll encounter it in:

  • Literary fiction and novels
  • Journalism and quality writing
  • Academic or professional contexts

You wouldn't typically say it out loud in casual conversation ("He was being totally surreptitious!") — that would sound a bit stiff. But in writing, it is a powerful, precise word that carries elegance.

If you ever need to recall this word quickly, remember this:

Surreptitious = secret + guilty awareness that it's wrong.

It's the word for every quiet, careful act done in the shadow of knowing you shouldn't be doing it.
15558:
Surreptitiously means doing something in a secret, careful, sneaky way — specifically because you know it is not allowed, or you know that others would disapprove or stop you if they noticed.

You are hiding what you are doing on purpose, and you are being careful about it.

There are really two things packed into this word at the same time:

  1. Secrecy — others do not know what you are doing.
  2. Awareness of wrongdoing — you know (or strongly sense) that the action is forbidden, disapproved of, or at least frowned upon. That is why you are hiding it.

This combination is what makes the word special. It is not just doing something in secret. It has a slightly guilty, sneaky quality to it. The person doing the action is conscious that they are doing something they probably should not be doing.

• During the exam, she surreptitiously glanced at her neighbor's paper.

(She was cheating — something not allowed — and she was being careful not to let the teacher see.)

  • He surreptitiously slipped a note to his friend during the board meeting.

(Passing notes during a formal meeting is not appropriate, so he did it quietly and carefully.)

  • The child surreptitiously grabbed a cookie from the jar while his mother had her back turned.

(He knew he was not supposed to have a cookie before dinner, so he was sneaky about it.)

  • She surreptitiously checked her phone during the movie.

(Using your phone in a cinema is considered rude, so she tried to do it without anyone noticing.)

Notice the common thread: in every case, the person knows they are doing something they are not supposed to, and they are being deliberate and careful about not getting caught.
How it differs from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so it is worth spending time here.

Secretly is a neutral, everyday word. It simply means "without others knowing." There is no suggestion of sneakiness or guilt. "She secretly admired his courage" — there is no wrongdoing here, just a private feeling. You would not say "surreptitiously" in this case, because she is not hiding something forbidden.

Stealthily focuses mainly on physical quietness and careful movement — like a cat creeping toward a bird. It is about how you move your body. It does not necessarily carry any moral weight or imply wrongdoing. A soldier moving stealthily through a forest is being quiet, not necessarily guilty.

Covertly is a more formal, professional word used mainly in military, government, or intelligence contexts. "The agents covertly gathered information." It is about operational secrecy. Personal guilt or sneakiness is not really the focus.

Discreetly is almost the opposite in feel, even though it involves not drawing attention. When you do something discreetly, you are being tactful and careful to avoid causing embarrassment or awkwardness — and this is generally seen as a good quality. "She discreetly reminded him that his microphone was still on." There is no wrongdoing at all; it is considered considerate behavior.

Furtively is the word most similar to surreptitiously, and they are often used interchangeably. The subtle difference: furtively tends to emphasize the nervous, anxious feeling of someone afraid of being caught — think of darting eyes, quick glances over the shoulder, jumpy behavior. Surreptitiously focuses more on the deliberate, careful act of concealing what you are doing. In practice, the difference is small, but if you picture someone stealing something, their behavior (nervous, shifty) is furtive, while their action (carefully sliding it under their coat) is surreptitious.

Whenever you are unsure whether to use this word, ask yourself:

Is this person doing something they know they should not, or that others would object to — and are they carefully and deliberately hiding it?

If the answer is yes, surreptitiously is likely the right word.

This is a formal, sophisticated word. You will encounter it most often in writing — novels, journalism, essays, formal reports. In casual everyday speech, people would more naturally say "sneakily", "on the sly", or "behind someone's back."

If you use "surreptitiously" in a conversation or piece of writing, it signals careful, educated use of language. It is never wrong to use it; it just sounds more formal than its casual equivalents.

Can surreptitiously be used even when there is no real wrongdoing? Occasionally, yes — but even then, the feeling of wanting to hide something from others remains. For example: "She surreptitiously studied his face, trying to read his expression." She is not doing anything wrong, but she does not want him to notice that she is watching him carefully. That slight self-conscious concealment is what keeps the word appropriate here.

The core of the word is always: deliberate, careful concealment of an action, driven by the awareness that it would not be approved of if noticed.
15559:
When you describe something as surrogate, you are saying it is a substitute — something that steps in and performs the role of another thing or person that is absent, unavailable, or unable to do so itself.

The logic always looks like this: the original is missing or out of reach → something else steps in → that something else is surrogate.

Imagine a school where the regular teacher falls ill and cannot come in. A substitute teacher arrives to take their place for the day. That substitute is filling a surrogate role — they are not the real, original teacher, but they are standing in and doing what the original teacher would have done.

If you said "the class was led by a surrogate teacher," it would mean: a teacher who is not the regular one, but who is filling that position in their absence.
Where you will most commonly encounter this word

1. Surrogate mother (or surrogate parent)

This is the most widely known use. A surrogate mother is a woman who agrees to carry and give birth to a baby on behalf of another person or couple — typically because that person or couple cannot have a child on their own due to medical reasons. The surrogate mother is not the intended parent; she is performing the biological role of motherhood in place of someone else. After the birth, the child is raised by the intended parent(s).

2. Surrogate family / surrogate parent

These phrases describe people who are not your biological family but who play the role of family in your life — providing care, love, support, and belonging. For example, if someone moves to a new city far from home and finds deep emotional warmth in a close group of friends, those friends might be called a surrogate family. They are not family by blood or law, but they function as one. Similarly, a mentor who guides and supports someone who grew up without a father might be described as a surrogate father figure.

3. Surrogate decision-maker (legal/medical context)

In law and medicine, a surrogate decision-maker is someone who is officially authorised to make decisions on behalf of another person who is unable to make those decisions themselves — for example, an unconscious patient in a hospital, or someone with a severe cognitive disability. The surrogate speaks and decides in place of the person who cannot.

4. Surrogate endpoint (medical/scientific context)

In clinical trials and medical research, doctors sometimes cannot directly measure the outcome they care about most (for example, whether a drug prevents death from heart disease over 20 years — that takes too long). So they measure something else that is closely linked to it, like blood pressure or cholesterol levels. These stand-in measurements are called surrogate endpoints — they substitute for the real, harder-to-measure outcome.

5. Surrogate goal (psychology)

A surrogate goal is something a person pursues as a stand-in for a deeper desire they cannot directly satisfy. For example, someone who feels powerless in their personal life might channel that frustration into obsessively controlling some minor area — that minor area becomes a surrogate for the real, unmet need.
Three things that are always true when something is "surrogate"

1. There is an original. A surrogate mother implies there is an intended mother. A surrogate family implies there is a "real" family that is absent or missing. The word "surrogate" only makes sense when there is an original role or function being referred to.
  2. The original is absent, unavailable, or cannot function. The surrogate exists because there is a gap. If the original were fully present and doing its job, there would be no need for a surrogate.
  3. The surrogate performs the same (or similar) role. A surrogate doesn't just vaguely resemble the original — it steps into the same function. A surrogate parent provides parenting. A surrogate endpoint measures what the real endpoint would have measured. The substitution is role-specific, not random.

Not necessarily — the word itself carries no built-in judgment about quality or worth.

A surrogate mother, for instance, is not "lesser" in any moral sense. The word simply describes the nature of the role: it is a substitute role, not the original one.

That said, in some contexts, "surrogate" can carry a gentle undertone of incompleteness — the idea that something real or original is missing, and the surrogate, however meaningful, exists to fill a gap. When someone speaks of a "surrogate family," there is an implicit acknowledgment that the person lacks their original family. The surrogate family is real and meaningful in its own right, but the word acknowledges the absence behind it.

These three words are closely related. The differences are subtle but real:

  • Substitute is the most everyday, general-purpose word. You can substitute one ingredient in a recipe, or a player on a sports team. It covers almost any swapping of one thing for another, big or small.
  • Replacement often implies the original is gone permanently, and the new thing takes over fully and finally.
  • Surrogate is typically reserved for situations where the role being filled is weighty, personal, deeply human, or formally significant — parenting, family, legal decision-making, medical measurement. It has a more serious, formal tone. You would not say "I used an apple as a surrogate orange in this recipe" — that would sound odd. For everyday, light substitutions, "substitute" or "replacement" is more natural. "Surrogate" is for the meaningful, consequential kind.
Register: when and how people use this word

"Surrogate" is not casual slang. It is a formal, serious word, most at home in:

  • Legal and medical contexts (surrogate mother, surrogate decision-maker, surrogate endpoint)
  • Psychology and social science (surrogate goal, surrogate relationship, surrogate attachment)
  • Thoughtful, careful writing and speech — journalism, academic writing, formal discussions

Surrogate (adjective): Describing something or someone that stands in for, and performs the role of, an original that is absent or unavailable — especially when the role being filled is significant, personal, or formally important.

The surrogate is not the real thing, but it is doing the real thing's job.
